title: F3 Lightning: How Meta Accelerates Ads ML Features to Production at Scale
abstract: Facebook Feature Framework (F3) is Meta’s framework for authoring, compiling, and serving the machine learning features underlying ads ranking models, where a single request can require more than 20,000 features. We first presented F3 at AI @ Scale 2020 . F3 reduced execution computational costs by compiling all features into a single merged graph, but that graph also served as the release unit, so a single failure or invalid definition blocked the entire release pipeline. This post introduces F3 Lightning , an infrastructure layer built on top of F3 to resolve this challenge by decoupling feature releases from shared execution, so each feature is compiled, validated, deployed, and rolled back independently. The hardest part to solve was preserving F3’s efficiency improvements. Early per-feature release prototypes increased CPU usage because independent features no longer shared computation. We aimed to close this gap through four optimizations: stable computation identifiers, a single shared execution plan, one shared memory buffer across all features, and dense index mapping for direct array access. With F3 Lightning, comparable extraction features now reach production ~3.6x faster than the prior F3, with no increase in infrastructure compute cost. This shorter release cycle also enables more model iterations in the same period. A Primer on F3’s Shared Execution Architecture Production machine learning systems rarely consume raw data directly. Before a model can make a prediction, its feature-serving system may need to read stored signals, filter events to a time window, count or sum values, normalize them, and combine intermediate results. The simplest design to complete this work treats every feature as an independent function. That is easy to understand, but it becomes wasteful at scale, because features are not computationally independent. A seven-day click count and a seven-day impression count may read the same event source and apply the same time-window filter. A click-through rate feature may then reuse both results. Running each feature separately would repeat that filter, and every other shared step, on every request. F3 approached this differently, by representing feature extraction as a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Each node performs one unit of work, such as reading an input, applying a filter, or calculating an aggregation. An edge means one computation depends on the result of another. The graph’s outputs are the feature values a model consumes. Engineers author each feature independently in a high-level language. The F3 compiler turns each definition into a small graph, then merges the graphs for every feature a service uses into one merged graph (Figure 1). Where features share an operation, such as the seven-day filter above, the compiler collapses the duplicates into a single node. That shared work then runs once per request, not once for every feature that needs it. At runtime, feature extraction is a traversal of this merged graph. Figure 1: F3 consolidates all features into one merged graph. The Shared Graph Made Every Release All-or-Nothing F3’s merged graph shared computation efficiently, but it came with a major catch: The graph was also the release, and one malformed definition could hold back every other feature in the merged graph. Figure 2 illustrates this challenge. It shows seven independently authored features, A through G, where five definitions are valid, but D and G contain unrelated errors. The “Attempt 1” build fails on D, so none of the seven features ships. After D is corrected, the “Attempt 2” build reaches G and fails again. Only after both definitions are fixed in “Attempt 3” does the complete merged graph make it successfully to production. Figure 2: One failing feature blocks the entire release. title: Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit
abstract: At a glance Formal methods for everyday software. PDD Kit helps you turn your intent into a formal spec, then proves the code your agent writes for every input and uses tests where a proof can’t reach. It takes formal methods beyond niche, specialist work to engineers without a formal methods background and to everyday applications, like the full-stack web app shown here. Exhaustive line-by-line human review can become difficult to scale as AI agents generate increasingly large amounts of code. The plan is supposed to be the contract between you and a coding agent, but nothing actually forces the agent to follow it. The tests it writes usually check what it built, rather than what you asked for. PDD Kit makes the agent keep the plan. It works with you to turn your intent into a formal specification in Verus (opens in new tab) , proves the agent’s code meets that spec for every input, and falls back to tests where a proof can’t reach. We tried it on a full-stack web app. Inside GitHub Next’s Chopin (opens in new tab) , we used PDD Kit to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust (opens in new tab) storefront. Verus hardened the code and uncovered existing bugs, proving the absence of login bugs with respect to the specification. The developer reviewed the intent and never read the generated code line-by-line. The plan is the contract the agent should follow, but nothing constrains the agent to follow it. Coding agents now ship whole features in one sitting often spanning tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of lines of code. As a result, reading every line of the pull request doesn’t scale to this new way of work. Now, most teams invest in the plan and relevant testing instead: describe to an agent what they want, go back and forth until the plan and proposed tests look right, and hand them off to the agent for implementation. This plan or natural language spec is meant to be the contract that an agent holds. However, in practice, the agent can drift from it. It implements something slightly different, then writes tests that pass for its implementation rather than the code you intended it to write. Continuous integration (CI) grows due to a profusion of low quality and high quantity of tests, coverage looks healthy, and the gap between what you asked for and what shipped stays hidden until a bug report or a nasty edge case shows up. So, how do you reliably scale review as agents generate increasingly large amounts of code? Agent code fails in two ways a careful reviewer would usually catch: it leaves out something obviously necessary, or it does something obviously wrong. Tests alone don’t close that gap, because they only exercise a tiny slice of what a program can do. Closing it needs a different kind of machinery, which is where proofs come in. Review asks “does this look right?” A proof answers “is this right?” A mathematical proof shows that code meets its specification for every input, including the ones your test suite can miss. That provides stronger assurance for specified properties than testing alone, especially when line-by-line review isn’t practical. Proofs used to be too expensive for everyday software. You needed specialists, unfamiliar languages, proofs many times larger than the code, and proofs took years to develop, but two things have changed since. First, recent advances in coding agents have made it increasingly practical for them to help generate formal proofs from well-defined specs. Secondly, agents can now better help you write formal specs. We call this new software development paradigm Proof-Driven Development (PDD). PDD Kit is our toolkit for it. How PDD Kit works PDD Kit is to formal methods roughly what Spec Kit (opens in new tab) is to Spec-Driven Development. It runs as a partner inside Chopin (opens in new tab) , GitHub Next’s real-time, multiplayer planning environment, where a team and agents can plan in one shared document. title: Learn the rules: The hacker mindset
abstract: For some, rules pose limitations. For others, like Microsoft Research Manager Mike Walker, they’re opportunities. Walker’s fascination with rules and their role in the social order has allowed him to find success professionally and personally, from uncovering weaknesses in networked systems to redefining how computers are trained to fend off cyberattacks to pushing the limits of a reliable mode of transportation—the bicycle—in ultra-endurance racing. In this conversation with Principal Technical Program Manager Weishung Liu, Walker describes how his participation in hacker culture led him to a career building next-generation cyber defense, including his work developing the first all-machine hacking tournament. Along the way, he reflects on why effective security depends on understanding trust and context, what competitive hacking taught him about teamwork and collective intelligence, and how an early lesson reshaped his understanding of leadership. He also tackles an important question: are today’s networked systems any safer than they were a decade ago? So I have, I have a definite fascination with the rules, [LAUGHTER] but the thing you have to understand about the rules is that rules are a social construct. And I think that a lot of … in the computer security field, when, when people hear the word “security” and they think about the rules that the security system is imposing on them, every time a security system asks something of users, then you’re asking for their trust. And that trust is a precious commodity. And so when you squander user trust, then the security regime falls down. So I think it’s really important to understand the social context of rules instead of just having instant adjudication. title: Hamed Karimi wins ECML PKDD Test-of-Time Award
abstract: In Naples last month, at the European Conference on Machine Learning and Principles and Practice of Knowledge Discovery in Databases (ECML PKDD), Amazon senior applied scientist Hamed Karimi and colleagues won the 2026 ECML PKDD Test-of-Time Award for their 2016 paper “Linear convergence of gradient and proximal-gradient methods under the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition”. The award recognizes research published a decade earlier that has had a lasting impact. The paper, written with Julie Nutini and Mark Schmidt while Karimi was a postdoctoral researcher at the University of British Columbia, has helped to organize a previously scattered field of machine learning optimization and offers useful approaches to analyzing new training methods. “When we wrote the paper in 2016, we genuinely didn’t expect it to make a splash,” Karimi says. “We did not know that the result would become part of the way researchers analyze optimization in machine learning.” Karimi and his coauthors showed that the Polyak-Łojasiewicz condition, a 1963 mathematical inequality that had been largely overlooked in machine learning, can prove that the standard method for training machine learning models closes in on the best solutions quickly, even when many different solutions could work equally well. Because modern machine learning models rarely have a single best solution, the result helped close a long-standing gap between what training methods do in practice and what theory could guarantee. Optimization landscape In the classic supervised-machine-learning setting, a model’s billions of settings, or parameters, are adjusted so that the model’s outputs match labeled training data as closely as possible. The distance between the model’s output and the labeled data is measured with a loss function; the goal is to tune the parameters to minimize the loss. This tuning is done through optimization processes, the most common approach being gradient descent or one of its variants. One way to understand gradient descent is to visualize a topographic map with peaks, valleys, cliffs, and plateaus. The lowest points on the map represent minimal loss, with each step downhill toward these minima representing parameter adjustments that optimize toward fewer errors. Ideally, researchers would like to know the quickest path to the bottom. Theory suggests that the fastest path shrinks the error by a constant fraction each step, a property known as linear convergence. The problem is that linear convergence is mathematically guaranteed only for a particular topographic shape: a steep bowl that uniformly curves upward, one that is strongly convex. A bowl like this has exactly one lowest point, so from any location, there is a single best move toward optimization. But many real problems don't work that way. When training data are redundant, as is the case with modern large language models, where the parameter count is disproportionately large compared to the amount of training data, the bottom of the landscape becomes a flat valley floor instead of a single point at the bottom of a bowl. These models — which exhibit weaker conditions than convexity — can be successfully trained with gradient descent, but the theory could neither explain why nor say how quickly, leaving a gap between what works in practice and what can be proven. By 2016, some 25 years’ worth of solutions to optimization problems with weaker conditions were in circulation, each with its own name, notation, and paper, but nobody had established how they related. Karimi and his colleagues’ paper settled those relationships. Researchers have since used variations of the paper’s method to rederive guarantees for essentially every standard optimization algorithm in machine learning. The paper has been cited over 2,000 times and has found a place in graduate textbooks. title: Getting started with Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: Today, we are announcing the general availability of Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. With Web Answer, agent builders get a synthesized, source-cited answer to a natural-language question with a single tool call. They no longer build a search, retrieve, synthesize, and citation pipeline themselves. If you have built agents that need to answer questions from current web sources, you know the pattern: call a search API, decide which results to trust, retrieve and clean page content, prompt a model to synthesize, and engineer citation extraction so the output traces back to a source. Every step is code you maintain, and every step is another place things can go wrong: hallucination when evidence is insufficient, stale content when the index moves, and broken attribution when a claim and its source drift apart. The Web Answer collapses that entire pipeline into one request. You send a question. You get back a cited answer in seconds. In this post, we explain what Web Answer does, compare it with Web Search on AgentCore, show how it works and what it returns, and walk through adding Web Answer to a gateway and calling it from an agent. What Web Answer does Figure 1: Request flow from an agent through the Gateway to Web Answer and back Your agent sends a question to your AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The Gateway authenticates the call with AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM) or a JSON Web Token (JWT). The Gateway calls Web Answer, a managed connector that AWS owns, using its own service role. Web Answer plans its searches, runs several in parallel, and reads key pages to check the facts. When the evidence is insufficient, it searches again. It then writes an answer that ties each claim to its source URL. The Gateway returns the answer and its citations to your agent as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool result. Web Answer is a managed AgentCore Gateway tool that takes a natural-language question and returns a synthesized answer in seconds grounded in current web sources. Here is what you get back: A grounded, cited answer, where each grounded claim maps to a citation, with a source URL where one is available. Current sources. Web Answer runs new searches for every question, and its model is given today’s date so it can search for up-to-date information. Agentic search: Web Answer plans its own searches, runs several in parallel, reads pages to verify facts, and decides when it has enough evidence to answer. Responsible AI safeguards: Web Answer is designed and tested with responsible AI safeguards. Figure 2: Demo video showing how to add Web Answer to an AgentCore Gateway, from setup to a finished, cited answer How it differs from Web Search Web Answer and the Web Search tools both support retrieval use cases, with different levels of integration complexity. The dividing line is who runs the model: Web Search: Returns ranked URLs, titles, snippets, and metadata. You keep your own model and control the synthesis. Use Web Search when you want full control over how results are processed. Web Answer: Runs the model, the agentic retrieval loop, synthesis, and attribution for you. You get a finished, cited answer. Use Web Answer when the question is a sub-task inside a larger agent and you do not want to own a retrieval pipeline for it. Many customers will use both. An agent might use Web Search for broad research tasks where it needs raw results, and Web Answer for specific factual questions where it needs a quick, cited answer. Set up and invoke Web Answer Web Answer is a connector that AWS owns. You reference it by ID, and the Gateway handles the tool schema, parameter governance, endpoint resolution, and authentication to the backend. In this walkthrough, you give your Gateway’s service role permission to call Web Answer, add a Web Answer target, and call it from a Strands agent. Getting started Getting started takes minutes. title: How Amazon Marketplace evaluates content quality with Amazon SageMaker AI
abstract: A+ Content is the rich media widget on the Amazon product detail page. Through visual assets, brands communicate unique product and brand value to help customers make informed purchase decisions. Selling partners using high-quality A+ Content boost their sales by 8–20 percent compared to those without it. A wide variety of brands, from established brands with large in-house design teams to bootstrapped brands with limited resources, use A+ Content, creating inconsistency in content quality. A typical A+ Content project combines text, images, and video into a cohesive product story. Evaluating each asset in isolation misses the quality that emerges from how those assets work together. When your content spans multiple heterogeneous modules and you need a holistic quality signal rather than per-asset checks, the multi-model fusion approach described in this post can help. In this post, we examine this problem in the context of A+ Content. A+ Content provides creative freedom for selling partners to express their authentic selves on their product detail pages, without strict content specifications such as image ratio and text word count. Although this flexibility allows compelling brand storytelling, it also creates substantial variation in content composition and quality. With quality evaluation and improvement recommendations, brands can transform average content into high-quality content that is more coherent, relevant, and useful. This improved content helps customers make more informed purchasing decisions and build lasting relationships with brands, leading to improved revenue for selling partners. To achieve this goal, an evaluation system must assess the complete content experience, provide actionable recommendations beyond numeric scores, and reflect the nuances across product categories. Existing approaches struggle to meet all these requirements simultaneously, so in this post, you will see a new approach using Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to understand and evaluate content holistically, and a diffusion-based generation component that produces improved visual assets from the resulting quality signals. In this post, you will learn how to: Render complete ecommerce content as a single snapshot and evaluate it holistically with a VLM. Combine VLM semantic scores with OCR readability signals in a lightweight CatBoost classifier trained on expert annotations. Use SHAP to explain quality decisions and generate actionable improvement recommendations for selling partners. Implement the end-to-end pipeline on Amazon SageMaker AI, from data ingestion and annotation through model hosting, explainability, and production monitoring. Opportunities and challenges in VLM-based evaluation A vision language model (VLM) pairs an image encoder with a large language model (LLM). The encoder, often a vision transformer (ViT) , splits an image into patches and turns them into embeddings, and a small connector maps those embeddings into the language model’s input space ( Flamingo , LLaVA ). Many VLMs reuse the image encoder from CLIP , which learned to match images with their captions. Because VLMs are trained to follow instructions, you can give one an image along with a rubric of evaluation criteria and get back a written assessment without task-specific training. When you need closer agreement with human reviewers, you can fine-tune the model on labeled examples. This makes VLMs a practical starting point for checking product images against your content guidelines at scale. Conventional computer vision models can already score individual assets, for example flagging a blurry image or a grammar error in a bullet list. Using a VLM to grade each asset separately adds little beyond that. A product detail page, however, combines images, text, and layout modules into a single story, and its quality depends on how those pieces work together. title: Use decision models with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations
abstract: Some of the questions you ask when evaluating an agent are narrow and repeatable. Did this response stay on policy? Is this tool call safe to approve? Does this answer match the retrieved context? Decision models answer exactly that kind of question. They take a structured state and a fixed set of allowed answers and return a calibrated probability over them, rather than free-form text whose confidence drifts from run to run. That makes them a strong fit for the scoring step in an agent evaluation, where you want a label and a number you can threshold and trust. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, scores an agent through its entire lifecycle, on demand during development, in batch jobs against stored sessions, and online against production traffic. Alongside 15 built-in evaluators, AgentCore Evaluations supports custom evaluators that you define as either an LLM-as-a-judge or a code-based evaluator. Custom LLM-as-a-judge evaluators apply your instructions and rating scale with a model in Amazon Bedrock. Code-based evaluators run your own logic in an AWS Lambda function, and that logic can call your choice of external system, model, or API, including a decision model. Decision models suit questions with a fixed set of answers that an informed person could decide at a glance, such as whether the agent refused a request or whether a response stayed on topic. After you validate a question on your own traffic, a decision model can be sufficient for that decision or score, and you can extend the same approach to specific harmfulness or stereotyping categories in your policy. Because both backends can answer several questions about the same state in a single request, you can use them as a screening layer rather than a replacement, running a pass or fail signal across your metrics to select the turns that warrant deeper assessment by the built-in evaluators, whose explanations help you investigate what went wrong. This post shows how to connect two decision model backends to AgentCore Evaluations through code-based evaluators. The first is Jev , a hosted decision model from TypeSafe. The second is Strands Decider 2B , an open-source decision model you run yourself. By the end of this post, you will know how to convert the AgentCore evaluator input into a decision model request, and the model’s probabilities back into an AgentCore evaluation result. First, though, when should you reach for a custom LLM-as-a-judge evaluator, and when does a decision model fit better? The next section breaks down what a decision model is and the trade-offs involved. Decision models A decision model is a small, specialized model trained to select from a fixed set of options and return calibrated confidence scores rather than generating free-form text. A general-purpose large language model (LLM) evaluator produces a score with a rationale. A decision model instead produces a probability distribution over predefined answers. That gives you a direct confidence measure you can threshold, aggregate, and act on programmatically. This makes decision models well-suited for evaluation tasks where the judgment can be stated as a choice among a fixed set of options: “Is this response grounded?” or “Did the agent complete the user’s goal?” Decision models are most useful when you want a well-calibrated confidence score alongside the label, not just a binary judgment. They are also appropriate when you want to enforce a specific rubric consistently without relying on a general-purpose LLM to interpret it. Jev, the hosted decision model from TypeSafe, and Strands Decider , an open-source, 2-billion-parameter decision model from the Strands Agents team, both support three types of questions. A noul question poses a yes/no question and returns a probability between 0 (no) and 1 (yes). A choice question asks which of up to 255 options applies, returning the most probable option along with the full distribution and a confidence

title: Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick: Human oversight where it matters
abstract: How should security leaders preserve human oversight as AI agents take on more work? Permissions establish which actions agents can take, but a permitted action can still warrant a person’s judgment. Requiring approval for every step might seem like the safest approach, yet multi-step tasks can produce repeated prompts , even for routine actions. Research on security warnings shows that attention and adherence can decline with repetition. The challenge isn’t to require more approvals, but to preserve attention for decisions that need human review. Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick addresses this challenge by reviewing eligible actions within your existing controls. It evaluates each proposed action against the user’s request and either approves it automatically or returns it to the user for review. It does this without granting additional permissions or removing required human approvals. Security leaders retain control over which actions must always go to a person, while Smart Approvals is designed to reduce unnecessary interruptions in routine work. Figure 1: Policy determines eligibility. Smart Approvals approves eligible actions or returns them to the user for review. Policy denials remain blocked Policy sets the boundary Quick evaluates each proposed action against Custom Permissions, Quick Guardrails, connector action permissions, and the user’s settings before automated review. Denied actions remain denied, and mandatory human approvals still apply. With Smart Approvals enabled, an action is eligible only when the user’s setting is “Ask each time” and no other control requires human approval. Connector action permissions, configured when a connector is created, can require human approval for specific actions. Administrators use Custom Permissions to determine who can use Smart Approvals. It’s on by default, but profiles with deny-by-default enabled must explicitly allow it. Users can also turn Smart Approvals off for themselves. That choice applies across conversations and scheduled runs. When it’s off, actions otherwise eligible for automated review require the user’s approval, and no account-level setting can turn it back on for them. How eligible actions are reviewed Smart Approvals uses a separate model, the classifier, to evaluate eligible actions against the user’s request and a bounded view of the conversation. It considers what the action does, where data goes, and who it affects. It can consult the user’s knowledge graph, which contains people and working relationships drawn from connected sources. This helps it understand how recipients relate to the user, such as whether a recipient is in the user’s reporting chain. This lookup stays within your Quick account. Quick doesn’t use the content the classifier reviews, including knowledge graph data, to train models or improve the service. An action can match the request and still warrant human review. Examples include sending content outside the organization or to senior leaders in the user’s reporting chain, changing access, deleting records, or initiating payments. This list isn’t complete, and the classifier also weighs the surrounding context. Reviewing actions against the user’s request adds a check against indirect prompt injection, where instructions in retrieved content attempt to redirect the agent. Quick instructs both the agent and classifier to treat that content as information, not instructions. Model review can still make mistakes, so actions that must always receive human approval, including those that move sensitive data, should require it through connector action permissions. The classifier provides judgment. The permission service enforces authority. Each automatic approval is single-use, applies only to the exact action and parameters reviewed, and grants no ongoing permission. Quick labels automatic approvals in the conversation. title: Four layers of context engineering for production AI agents: How Deep Insight applies them in working code
abstract: When production AI agents handle tasks such as data analysis and report generation, context management can become a major bottleneck. A 200K-token window sounds generous until a real-world task burns through most of it in minutes. Data analysis and report generation leave the agent failing mid-execution, losing accuracy, or driving up costs. A body of published guidance already addresses this, but the individual techniques are easier to read about than to apply. Applied together, they make a measurable difference: in the reference implementation this post walks through, a single write-and-execute tool cuts the tokens each script adds to context by about 95 percent, and loading skills on demand shrinks the system prompt by about 97 percent. This series organizes that guidance into practices you can apply directly. Anthropic’s engineering posts, together with features built into the Strands Agents SDK, converge on four layers of context engineering: isolate context at the architecture level, control it through prompts, externalize it to the filesystem, and verify it with independent agents and safeguards. In this post (Part 2), you will learn how each layer works and what it looks like in working code. We applied these techniques in Deep Insight , an open source multi-agent data analysis solution built on the Strands Agents SDK and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which serves as the reference implementation throughout. Post series Part 1: 5 production challenges in multi-agent systems and how Deep Insight solved them. Part 2: Four layers of context engineering for production AI agents: How Deep Insight applies them in working code. Part 3: Harness engineering in practice: moving Deep Insight from dev to production. (Coming soon!) The first post defined five core challenges that production multi-agent systems must solve. It introduced how Strands Agents SDK , Amazon Bedrock and Bedrock AgentCore , and AWS Fargate each address different layers of the problem, with code examples. This second post takes the four layers of context engineering practice that sit on top of that architecture and shows each one implemented. The third post guides you through deploying and operating agents in a secure private network on Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), covering everything needed for real-world operations. What is context engineering? Context engineering is the discipline of optimizing the information in a large language model (LLM)’s limited context window so agents perform at their best. Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.5, available on Amazon Bedrock, offers a 200K context window, but complex production tasks quickly exceed it. For example, a seemingly straightforward request like “ Analyze sales data and create a DOCX report ” runs through several stages: data loading and exploration (5 min), category-based sales analysis (3 min), generating five charts for time-series analysis (10 min), statistical validation (3 min), and final report generation (5 min). Together they consume over 150K tokens across 15 minutes. Processing such tasks in a single context causes problems: the window overflows mid-task, stale context degrades performance, and errors require re-running the whole pipeline. As context grows, attention to important information drops, and inefficiency raises cost under per-token pricing. “As the number of tokens in the context window increases, the model’s ability to accurately recall information from that context decreases (Context rot).” — Anthropic, “ Effective Context Engineering for AI Agents ” (2025.09) Context engineering solves exactly these problems, and it is not only a collection of techniques. Spanning architecture design, prompt writing, tool implementation, and verification, it’s a layered discipline where each layer compensates for what the previous ones miss. title: How Indegene is modernizing and scaling enterprise data quality in life sciences
abstract: This post is co-written with Shravan K S from Indegene Limited. Enterprise AI is creating new opportunities for life sciences organizations to improve decision-making across commercial, medical, market access, and other business functions. But the quality of every AI model, dashboard, and business insight depends on one thing: trusted data. As enterprise data grows across multiple platforms, pipelines, and business domains, maintaining consistent data quality has become increasingly difficult. Manual data quality rule creation, fragmented governance, and evolving business definitions make it challenging to scale data quality across the enterprise. This post explores how Indegene built a production-grade, large language model (LLM) powered Data Quality Agent within its NEXT Unified Data Platform (NEXT UDP) on AWS. The agent generates context-aware data quality rules, validates them, and produces ready-to-run SQL and Python code under centralized, human-in-the-loop governance. Together, these capabilities help organizations improve data quality at enterprise scale while reducing the effort required to build and maintain data quality programs. About Indegene Indegene Limited (BSE: 544172, NSE: INDGN) is the strategic operating partner to the life sciences industry, orchestrating commercial, medical, R&D, and safety operations across the product lifecycle. Trusted by the world’s top 20 biopharma companies, Indegene helps run complex, highly regulated workflows at global scale. Indegene combines deep life sciences expertise with AI-embedded platforms and governed operating models to improve speed, consistency, and compliance across mission-critical operations. By integrating technology into how work is executed and scaled, Indegene helps life sciences organizations deliver measurable outcomes in regulated environments. Why conventional data quality programs break down Most organizations have established data quality processes but keeping them effective is becoming increasingly difficult as enterprise data ecosystems evolve. One of the biggest challenges is the divide between technical and business rule ownership. Data engineers typically define technical rules that confirm whether data is structurally correct. For example, verifying that an HCP ID (Healthcare Professional ID) isn’t null, follows the required format, is unique, and maps to a valid reference record. Business teams define rules that determine whether the data makes sense in its operational context. For example, confirming that product market share totals 100 percent within a territory or that an HCP’s prescription activity aligns with their specialty and eligibility criteria. Because technical rules are often maintained in code while business rules reside in glossaries, SOPs, and subject-matter expertise, keeping them aligned and consistently governed across datasets and platforms becomes difficult. Traditional validation techniques also have inherent limitations. Checks for null values, data types, uniqueness, or referential integrity remain essential, but they can’t capture business-specific context. Validating product hierarchies, customer segmentation, territory alignment, or commercial business rules requires domain knowledge that static validation logic can’t easily represent. Creating and maintaining data quality rules is equally demanding. Every new dataset requires data profiling, rule definition, SQL development, validation, and ongoing maintenance. These rules are often spread across SQL scripts, pipeline code, spreadsheets, data catalogs, and tool-specific configurations. As schemas, business definitions, or validation thresholds change, the effort required to update and govern these rules grows significantly. Additionally, the operational impact is significant. title: How U Mobile built agentic telco operations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: U Mobile, Malaysia’s newest 5G network provider, has always run its telco operations lean, doing more with less through continuous automation. When new AI capabilities became available, U Mobile explored how to enhance operational efficiency beyond basic productivity gains. The real opportunity was further upstream, in how operations teams diagnose and resolve problems in the first place. The same lean operating discipline shaped the foundation for AiDaH: not a one-off technology initiative, but the next step in a long-running journey to simplify operations and scale capability without adding complexity. When a subscriber can’t purchase a data add-on, resolving it isn’t a single problem. It’s a coordination problem. A customer service agent needs to pull interface logs for error codes. The same agent must then query business support system APIs for subscriber eligibility, and cross-reference internal knowledge bases for applicable business policies. All of that happens across multiple systems, before drafting a single word of response. And when that fails, the ticket escalates to backend IT teams and the subscriber waits even longer. Traditional automation tools can help agents write better responses. What they can’t do is navigate multiple systems, analyze the results, and propose corrective action. Closing that gap takes an agentic architecture built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. U Mobile’s Information Systems Division (ISD) built exactly that. Working with AWS and AWS Partner Axrail, they created AiDaH, the AI-Driven Agentic Helpdesk, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Two capabilities decided the choice. The managed agent runtime meant there was no agent infrastructure to operate. Built-in memory carried conversational context across turns without standing up a separate state store. Within a year of starting the journey, AiDaH handles over 150 documented operational scenarios across six business divisions. U Mobile’s internal measurements show trouble ticket volumes falling by up to 84.5 percent in key categories. In this post, we walk through the six-layer architecture behind AiDaH. We then describe the security foundation beneath the platform, and close with a brief note on the spec-driven method the team used to build it. The problem: Too many systems, too much friction U Mobile’s IT landscape reflects the complexity typical of modern telecommunications: business support and customer relationship management systems, mobile number portability platforms, big data analytics, and infrastructure monitoring tools, running hybrid across on-premises and cloud. Before AiDaH, this fragmentation meant that even routine diagnoses required manually checking logs, querying subscriber eligibility, and consulting knowledge bases for business policies, across separate systems and portals. Each lookup was a context switch, each context switch was time lost, and each unresolved query became an escalation to a backend IT team. Expanding coverage to additional operational domains compounded the problem, because every new system typically required a bespoke integration. The ISD team’s strategy rested on three pillars. Reach : agents that coordinate across backend systems in real time. Depth : chain-of-thought reasoning for multi-step root cause analysis. Community : a secure multi-tenant framework with role-based access control and built-in guardrails, available to every division. The journey: From knowledge base to agentic platform AiDaH started with a principle: think big, start small. U Mobile began conceptualization in late 2025 with two pilot agents and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, a fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capability. A Q1 2026 pilot brought the internal IT helpdesk online with 4 agents and 20 operational scenarios. title: Bring structured and unstructured data together with Amazon Quick
abstract: Organizations collect data in many forms. Structured data lives in databases and spreadsheets, whereas unstructured data sits in documents, reports, and files stored across file systems. Analyzing both together typically requires switching between multiple tools, running separate queries, and manually correlating results. Amazon Quick addresses this with a unified experience. You can connect structured data through enriched datasets and unstructured data through S3-backed knowledge bases . You can then query both through a single conversational AI agent. In this post, you learn how to: Connect Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) as a data source and create a knowledge base. Build a Space that combines structured and unstructured data. Create and configure a custom chat agent that queries across both data types. Ask questions that span structured and unstructured sources in a single conversation. Solution architecture The following diagram illustrates how each component connects to deliver a unified data experience through Amazon Quick. Figure 1: Solution architecture for combining structured and unstructured data in Amazon Quick The architecture has three layers: Data layer: Your data exists in two forms. Unstructured content (documents, PDFs, reports) is stored in Amazon S3 and indexed through a knowledge base. Structured data (metrics, sales figures, and operational key performance indicators) is loaded as enriched datasets with semantic descriptions that the agent uses to translate questions into SQL. Workspace layer: A Space brings both data types together into a single workspace. The Space references your knowledge base for unstructured queries and your datasets for structured queries. It can also include dashboards, file uploads, and action connectors. This is the layer where data from different sources converges into a unified context. Agent layer: The custom chat agent links to the Space and uses it as its knowledge source. When a user asks a question, the agent determines whether to query the knowledge base, the dataset, or both, and returns a combined response with citations. Amazon Quick also applies built-in AI guardrails , such as content safety screening, to chat interactions. With this layered approach, you can expand the solution over time. When you add a new data source to the Space, the agent linked to that Space can use it, and responses respect the permissions of the user who asks. title: ServiceNow on-behalf-of token exchange with Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
abstract: AI agents that interact with enterprise APIs on behalf of users need to maintain user identity throughout the request chain. Without identity propagation, API calls arrive at downstream services as the application itself rather than the user who initiated the action. This breaks audit trails, bypasses user-level access controls, and violates the principle of least privilege. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This post shows how to configure AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, for an on-behalf-of (OBO) token exchange with Microsoft Entra ID. An AI agent can then call the ServiceNow REST API while preserving the calling user’s identity. You configure the token exchange on the gateway target, and AgentCore Gateway performs the exchange on each request. The pattern can be applied to other REST APIs protected by OAuth. In production, you can additionally pair identity propagation with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to filter harmful content and validate the agent’s inputs and outputs. Solution overview The architecture involves three key components connected through AgentCore Gateway: An AI agent application, protected by Microsoft Entra ID through an OAuth application registration. A Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, implemented using AgentCore Gateway, sitting between the agent and ServiceNow. The ServiceNow REST API, configured with an inbound OAuth integration tied to Microsoft Entra ID. The following figure shows the end-to-end solution architecture, including components within AWS, Microsoft Entra ID, and ServiceNow. Figure 1: Solution architecture across AWS, Microsoft Entra ID, and ServiceNow As shown in Figure 1, the user acquires a JSON Web Token (JWT) to invoke the agent 1. The agent authenticates to the gateway with a JWT token scoped to the agent’s own application registration 2. The gateway then exchanges that token, using the OBO flow, for a new token scoped to the ServiceNow API connector, with the original user’s identity preserved 3. ServiceNow receives a valid token whose preferred_username claim maps to an existing ServiceNow user and applies that user’s permissions to the API call 4. How OBO token exchange works in this context When the agent calls the gateway, it presents a JWT with an audience claim matching the agent’s client ID (for example, 3ff88e17-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX ). ServiceNow, however, expects a token with an audience claim matching its own API connector client ID ( 5d4a7a11-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX ). The OBO flow bridges this gap. AgentCore Gateway sends the inbound token to the Entra token endpoint along with the agent application’s client credentials, the target scope, and a parameter requested_token_use: on_behalf_of . Entra validates that the calling user consented to the delegation, then issues a new token for the ServiceNow API with the original user’s claims intact. Prerequisites Before you begin, you need the following: An AWS account with access to AgentCore Gateway. A Microsoft Entra ID tenant with permissions to create application registrations . Your account needs at least the Application Developer role to register applications. A ServiceNow instance with administrative access to configure inbound OAuth integrations. You can create a ServiceNow personal developer instance (PDI) at the ServiceNow personal developer instance signup page https://developer.servicenow.com/ . title: Build a semantic layer for agentic AI with EDB Postgres AI and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: In this post, we show how to build a semantic layer for agentic AI using EDB Postgres AI . We run a Strands Agents agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that queries the layer to answer customer 360 (C360) questions. Earlier posts in this series built the same C360 pattern with Stardog’s knowledge graph , Denodo’s data virtualization platform , AtScale’s dimensional model , and Strategy Mosaic’s linked models . EDB Postgres AI puts the semantic layer inside the operational Postgres database as an AIDB extension . Business meaning lives next to the data in standard Postgres COMMENT statements, the join graph comes from Postgres foreign keys, and governance uses Postgres GRANT and row-level security through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint that ships with AIDB. By the end of this post you will know: How to build an AIDB semantic knowledge base (SemKB) over a Postgres schema, how COMMENT ON statements and aidb.create_semantic_alias behave as the authoring surface, and how foreign keys crawl into join paths. How to expose the AIDB tool catalog to an external agent through the built-in EDB MCP endpoint, fronted by an Application Load Balancer (ALB) and registered as an MCP target on AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. How Postgres roles, column-level GRANT statements, and row-level security produce different results for different callers. The prompt, tool catalog, and agent code stay the same. How AIDB captures OpenTelemetry traces for every SQL execution as rows in the aidb_otel schema, queryable with ordinary SQL. Three layers an agent needs An agent that answers business questions from live data needs three layers: a model that plans and writes queries, a meaning layer that tells the agent what the data represents, and a runtime that hosts the agent and controls identity and access. The Stardog post in this series introduced this framing. The model layer in this post is Anthropic Claude on Amazon Bedrock , the same as prior posts (model availability varies by AWS Region ). The runtime layer is AgentCore runtime , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. AgentCore Gateway handles inbound authorization, and AgentCore Identity , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, holds outbound credentials for the tool targets, same as prior posts. EDB Postgres AI hosts agents and tools inside the database itself and acts as the connection point for external agents through its MCP endpoint. The meaning layer is where this post diverges from the others. Here it is a SemKB that lives inside the operational Postgres database. The schema and the business definitions are indexed together. Postgres GRANT , row-level security, and column-level grants enforce access, not an advisory system prompt. The sections that follow cover how AIDB builds the layer, how AgentCore exposes it, and how two Postgres roles asking the same question get different answers. Example use case: C360 on EDB Postgres AI The dataset is the Stardog C360 Knowledge Kit , loaded into a single EDB Postgres AI instance in a dedicated c360 schema. The data model has four tables and one derived view. title: Building ultra-low-latency voice AI applications on AWS
abstract: Conversational AI is transforming how humans interact with technology. From virtual assistants and AI-powered contact centers to real-time translation and accessibility tools, voice-first interfaces are rapidly becoming the default mode of interaction for millions of users worldwide. Yet delivering a truly natural voice experience remains one of the hardest challenges in AI infrastructure. Users expect human-like responsiveness. Excess latency can break conversational flow and erode trust. To feel natural, AI-generated speech must arrive within the same temporal window as human turn-taking. This post introduces how Cartesia , an AWS Partner specializing in real-time voice AI, uses purpose-built State Space Models (SSMs) and AWS infrastructure to deliver sub-100ms text-to-speech and speech-to-text at global scale. Developers can build voice experiences that feel indistinguishable from human conversation. The rise of conversational AI and latency expectations The demand for real-time voice AI is growing rapidly across industries: Contact centers: AI agents handling millions of customer interactions require instantaneous speech generation to maintain natural dialogue. Telehealth: Remote patient consultations demand low-latency voice for accurate, empathetic communication. Gaming and virtual worlds: Immersive experiences require real-time voice synthesis for non-player characters (NPCs) and player interactions. Accessibility: Screen readers and voice interfaces must respond instantly to serve users with visual impairments. Inbound and outbound sales: AI sales agents must respond without awkward pauses to qualify leads, handle objections, and keep prospects on the line. Traditional transformer-based text-to-speech (TTS) models struggle with streaming latency because they process entire sequences before producing output. This architectural limitation creates a fundamental tension: higher quality often means higher latency. A new class of models, State Space Models, resolves this trade-off. AI for voice: State Space Models (SSM) State Space Models (SSMs) take a fundamentally different approach to processing sequences than transformers, the architecture behind most of today’s AI. Transformers use a mechanism called attention, which compares every element in a sequence to every other element. As a result, the amount of computation grows quadratically as the sequence gets longer. SSMs instead treat a sequence as a system that evolves continuously over time, processing it step by step and carrying a compact internal state forward. This can be converted into a form computers handle efficiently, keeping the cost low for certain long sequences. This efficiency makes SSMs well suited to real-time, streaming data like live speech. Key advantages of SSMs for audio processing include: High-quality long-range dependencies: Structured SSMs are a form of linear recurrence, but their state parameterization preserves information over long audio sequences, avoiding the long-range signal decay that limits classic recurrent neural networks (RNNs) such as long short-term memory (LSTM) networks. Constant memory footprint: Unlike transformers that cache all previous tokens, SSMs maintain a fixed-size hidden state. Native streaming support: The recurrent structure processes input token-by-token, so it supports true streaming without architectural modifications. These properties make SSMs uniquely suited for real-time voice applications where both quality and latency are non-negotiable. How it works: SSMs for real-time voice Cartesia puts these SSM advantages to work in two production voice models: Sonic for speech generation and Ink for transcription. Introducing Cartesia Cartesia is a real-time multimodal intelligence company that has built a voice AI application, purpose-built on State Space Model architecture. title: Introducing India-based inference for Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Kimi K3 is a multi-modal, open-weight foundation model (FM) that provider Moonshot AI reported achieved frontier-level coding and general agentic intelligence at release. In addition to global and US-based inference, Amazon Bedrock now supports in-country inference in India for Kimi K3: unblocking local workloads with strict data residency requirements. Customers like Ultrahuman are already seeing the benefits in production: “Jade, an AI Health and Wellness assistant in the Ultrahuman app, answers questions in plain language using each person’s own Ring and glucose data, across more than 14,000 conversations a day. Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock let us add a leading open-weight model through the API we already use, with health data staying inside AWS and Mumbai as a fallback Region. With prompt caching, we’ve cut LLM costs by 80 percent and made multi-turn chats 85 percent faster.” — Aditya Patawari, VP Engineering, Ultrahuman In this post, we explain the different global and geographic inference options available, and share code for an example use case: optical character recognition (OCR) and understanding of Indic-language documents, with follow-up question answering in code-mixed Hinglish. Choose where inference can run Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock is offered through cross-Region inference profiles . You can invoke the model from any of a wide range of AWS Regions (the “source”). Amazon Bedrock then securely processes your request in one of multiple possible “destination” Regions. Cross-Region inference is fully managed by AWS: Data is encrypted in transit between Regions and remains on the AWS network, never traversing the public internet or requiring you to set up any multi-Region virtual private cloud (VPC) infrastructure. The inference profile ID you invoke controls which destination Regions are eligible: Profile Model ID When to choose it Global global.moonshotai.kimi-k3 Recommended for most use cases: lowest cost and most broadly available India geographic in.moonshotai.kimi-k3 Inference processing must stay within Mumbai and Hyderabad Regions See the Amazon Bedrock Kimi K3 model card for up-to-date information on available inference profiles, which AWS Regions they can be called from, and what destination Regions they can use for inference. Example walkthrough: Indic-language document understanding Let’s consider an example use case: reading a scanned Hindi document, extracting structured data, and answering follow-up questions in mixed Hindi and English (Hinglish). This need is common in Indian financial services and public sector workflows where know your customer (KYC) forms, utility bills, and similar documents must often be digitized. Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock can directly read and reason about images, including those containing multilingual text. It offers a potential solution with no separate OCR or translation service required. Prerequisites The full source code for this example is available on GitHub . To follow along, you need: An AWS account . Python 3.11 or later installed, with internet access to install the required PyPI packages . The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) installed, with credentials configured with sufficient AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to invoke the Kimi K3 model through the India inference profile. The New Knowledge Artifacts of the AI Economy
abstract: At our recent Foo Camp , a number of people said something like, “I don’t want someone else’s code any more. I may have my agent take a look at it, but I want to extract just the parts that I want, and may rewrite even those in Rust. It’s just too easy to create just the code that I want.” This topic was hot enough that Jesse Vincent held an entire session about it. I did not attend, but Jesse gave me a report from his Plaude AI notetaker. Here’s a relevant section of the summary: Several participants argue that software development’s primary artifact may be shifting from executable code toward natural-language prompts, generation processes, and developer skills. One speaker compares Python to assembly language, suggesting that writing conventional code may become optional as natural-language generation takes precedence. Another argues that open source can survive such a transition because its core values—peer production, capacity building, and shared specifications—do not depend on who or what writes the code. At the same time, Jesse warns that maintainers are overwhelmed by floods of uninvited, automated, and often low-quality contributions. Participants say that traditional milestones such as pull requests, repositories, and conferences have helped contributors connect and gain recognition; as AI makes code replication easier, communities may need new ways to acknowledge participation and create paths for future developers. Some community interaction has moved to spaces such as Discord and direct messages, but structured opportunities are still needed. Scientific computing raises particular concerns. One panelist warns that AI-generated forks and agent attacks could threaten carefully verified foundations such as NumPy and SciPy. Scientific systems depend on battle-tested libraries and reproducibility, so thousands of unreviewed alternatives could undermine reliability. Participants suggest bridging traditional open-source communities and modern AI development, which currently may use different tools and artifacts. Other proposals include treating code as “liquid” and focusing open-source governance on durable infrastructure and specifications; maintaining agent storage independently of ephemeral container lifecycles; and using corporate compliance and safety-monitoring architectures to aggregate organizational traces. These are important observations, all pointing in the same direction: AI is transforming the mechanisms and the artifacts of software development. For an increasing number of use cases, the software source code itself may no longer be the most important shareable knowledge artifact. This isn’t a new phenomenon. Every major change in technology calls for new mechanisms, new artifacts, and new institutions. Originally, software developers mostly distributed binaries, then open source developers made sharing source code the norm. Now we need to distribute and share something else: context and patterns for generating code on the fly. Knowledge is being unbundled and can be shared in new forms. A repo may now serve merely as a source of context for solving the exact problem I have, rather than the bundle of problems that the original developer(s) encoded into their library or packaged solution. Some people will keep their context and patterns private, either because they see proprietary advantage in keeping them to themselves or because they are too busy or too lazy to share. But part of the problem is that we haven’t yet figured out what needs to be shared! The challenge for the software development community is to identify the new knowledge artifacts of the AI economy, and to build new mechanisms and incentives for sharing them. We’ve all had the experience of seeing a bespoke agentically generated app, wanting something similar, and wishing we could ask for a starting point so we didn’t have to vibe code an equivalent from scratch, with all the attention, false starts, and token costs that comes with that. title: What It Takes To Trust Automatic Model Routing
abstract: When a new coding model comes out, I want to try it. New releases always carry a promise for me. Maybe it can handle a change that needed too much manual intervention before. Maybe it can find the problem an earlier model kept missing. Maybe it can handle some coding scenarios that my favorite model can’t handle today. To discover a new model’s capabilities, I need to spend time with it to find out what I can reasonably hand over to it. Having said all that, I understand the frustration when a new model becomes available, but your assistant won’t let you choose that model. Somebody has decided which models you can use and when you can use them. You are left trying to decide whether the answer is good enough and can’t get your hands on the new shiny toys. At the same time, I’m quite happy to let an assistant choose a model if that makes my budget last longer. New toys tend to be expensive and top-line models don’t make a difference here. There are plenty of steps in development where a cheaper model might do everything required. Using it for those steps could leave more of the budget available for a difficult investigation later. If routing lets me keep using capable assistance throughout the day, I have a good reason to use it. I want routing to give me more assistance for the same budget. The quality of that assistance depends on how the models, tools, and context handling fit together. And I need enough information about what the assistant did to judge the result. Getting more help from the same budget A fixed AI budget puts a fairly ordinary constraint on a team. Or better, on the affected individual. You have an amount you can spend, and of course you want as much help as possible from it. Each request uses some of that amount. And it really gets frustrating when repeating a request, correcting an answer, and asking the assistant to try again consume even more of the budget. Automatic routing gives the system a way to manage that spending for you. It can use a cheaper model where that model is likely to succeed and spend more where the additional capability is likely to help. You, the developer, can then concentrate on the task while the assistant handles some of these decisions and you don’t have to constantly worry about which model to pick for which task. The researchers behind RouteLLM trained routers to choose between a stronger model and a cheaper one using preference data. They reported more than a twofold reduction in cost with minimal impact on response quality on the benchmarks they evaluated. You still need to check how it performs on your own tasks. The next question is how those savings get to me in my day-to-day jobs. If requests become cheaper to serve, the same subscription could support more of them. A team could keep its assistant available to more people within an existing spending limit. The saving could also make it practical to use a more capable model more often when the task calls for it. So much for the theory. In most assistants that behavior is little more than a “switch.” That connection to better results needs to be visible in the product. If I choose automatic routing, I want to understand what I get from it. Perhaps I can send more requests before I reach a limit. The results still need to meet my expectations, of course. This is a fairly reasonable thing to ask of a feature that spends part of the budget on my behalf. The time we spend with the assistant belongs in that calculation too. Think about how a cheaper request can lead to another attempt, followed by another explanation, followed by a correction. If this happens often enough, I spend more time getting the code ready to accept than I would have with a more capable model. So when we compare routing policies, we need to follow the task through those interactions. Then we can look at both the money spent and the time we put into getting there and compare both together. title: Resonant Computing and Common Fabric
abstract: This event summary was created by Claude with editing by Tim O’Reilly, based on a transcript of the conversation. Alex Komoroske is the CEO and a cofounder of Common Fabric , a public benefit corporation building the infrastructure for human-centric agentic computing. He spent more than a decade at Google as a product manager and director of product management on Chrome, Google Maps, and Google Earth, and he later ran corporate strategy at Stripe. At O’Reilly’s AI Codecon a year earlier, in a talk called “ Why Centralized AI Is Not Our Inevitable Future ,” he argued that we were sleepwalking into the wrong future for AI and didn’t have to accept it. Since then he has coauthored the Resonant Computing Manifesto , which Tim signed. On Tuesday, October 20, 2026, Tim O’Reilly hosted Alex for an hour-long conversation, “ Can We Build More-Human Technology? ” Common Fabric’s consumer product hasn’t yet been released, but Alex showed Tim the product privately the day before, and Tim said his conversations with Alex had left him “more optimistic about the future of the web and the AI future than I’ve been in a long time.” They talked about the underlying theory behind Common Fabric. The Resonant Computing Manifesto The Resonant Computing Manifesto lays out five principles for resonant technology. It is private , meaning you’re the steward of your own data and it’s used in accordance with your wishes. It is dedicated , with no conflicts of interest. It is plural , with no central entity holding an unnecessary amount of power. It is adaptable , able to do things its creators didn’t specifically build in. And it is prosocial , helping people create meaning together rather than living as “individual islands.” According to Alex, the manifesto rests on a distinction between two kinds of experience. A hollow thing is something that you like when you’re using it, and then, after you’re done using it, you’re left feeling regret. And a resonant thing is something that you like when you’re using it, and then afterwards you’re left feeling nourished. They are superficially very similar, but they’re fundamentally, deeply, structurally different. Alex argued that modern tech, business, and politics are very good at delivering hollow experiences efficiently and poor at delivering resonant ones. The manifesto came from a group of people who still believe in the hacker ethic of the 1990s and early 2000s, he said. They believe that technology is a large positive force for humanity, but also that the industry has spent the last decade optimizing for engagement and extraction, which has undermined that positive impact. They think that the AI transition is a unique opportunity to reset the norms and the architecture to make something that works better for people than for extractive business models. Privacy, bits, and the physics of trust Tim started out by asking Alex to go a bit deeper on privacy. Privacy and trust are related in ways the privacy movement often doesn’t consider, Tim said. We don’t put bars on all of our windows. We trust most people not to break in because we built a society where trust is the norm. It’s held in place not just by penalties but by social rewards for people who follow norms. “People will think you’re a creep if you go look into somebody’s window,” Tim noted. Like bars on the window, hard privacy seems to Tim a bit like an admission that we’re giving up on positive social norms and penalties for rulebreakers (where needed). He wanted to know whether Alex meant “private” in the way that HIPAA makes your healthcare records private, where your data is made hard for anyone to see, including you. Alex doesn’t mean that at all. He means privacy that makes your data more useful by putting it under your control. He gave a three-part answer about how that happens. title: Measuring AI’s Impact on Delivery Speed
abstract: The following article was originally published on James Shore’s Successful Software blog and is being republished here with the author’s permission. Is AI making software development faster? Most people I talk to say yes. But how much? What value are you getting for your money? Are there other ways of using AI that have a better ROI? This is part 2 of my series on assessing AI’s impact on software development. In part 1 , we looked at why assessing impact is important, and what not to do. In this part, we’re looking at how to measure AI’s impact on delivery speed. In part 3 , we’ll look at how to measure the unintended consequences of AI, before wrapping up the series in part 4 with an examination of business outcomes. Finally, an epilogue puts it all together with notes you can share with your CFO. What we’re measuring Delivery speed isn’t productivity. I’ll say it again, loud, for the folks in the back: Delivery speed isn’t productivity! It’s a component of productivity, sure. Given two equivalent teams creating the same piece of software, the team that delivers first is the one that’s more productive. But it’s not just about output. To my mind, software development productivity is value produced divided by money spent . It’s a strict definition but a useful one, because it gets to the heart of why we build software: to achieve some valuable purpose. Going faster doesn’t mean you’re going in the right direction. We’ll consider business outcomes in part 4 . For now, though, we’ll tackle a simpler question: Are your teams finishing their assigned work faster, regardless of whether that work is actually useful or not? The core approach First, the bad news: There’s no objective measure of software development speed. I can’t look at two teams and say, “This one is fast, and that one is slow.” That’s because none of the outputs teams create are standardized. We already talked in part 1 about how lines of code and PRs are bad metrics. Well, nothing else is standardized, either. Features? Some are big, some are small. Bugs? Some are easy, some are hard. Stories? Velocity? Story points? Completely arbitrary. They have way more to do with what’s being requested than the speed of the team. Okay, if they’re all different sizes, couldn’t we just use estimates? Surely if a team is constantly missing its estimates, it’s because it’s slow, right? Not so fast! Software estimates are famously inaccurate. A team that always misses its estimates isn’t slow. It’s just overly optimistic. Teams are nearly always overly optimistic. 1 So we can’t count requests (features, bugs, stories, etc.) because they vary in size, and we can’t look at on-time delivery, because estimates are overly optimistic. Sounds like a whole lotta “can’t.” What can we do? We can compare a team to itself. If a team’s estimates were perfectly consistent, and they went from taking 3x longer than estimated to 1.5x longer, then they’re twice as fast! Huzzah! If only it were that simple. There are a few snags. 2 Estimates aren’t consistent Snag the first: Teams’ actual estimate ratios aren’t actually consistent. Some are bigger, some are smaller. Plot them on a graph, and they form an “S” curve, as with this data from a real company. 3 If delivery speed improves, the curve will shift. Individual data points may be better or worse than the original approach, but you can see the effect in aggregate. 4 People work differently Second snag: Some people are pessimistic and estimate high. Some estimate low. Some people spend a lot of time educating others. Others work heads down as fast as possible. Some clean up messes. Others create messes. If you do a blanket comparison of everyone to each other, you introduce a lot of noise. Noise is bad because it increases the amount of data you have to collect. To keep things clean, compare people (or teams) to themselves. Estimates change when people know they’re using AI Third snag: People’s estimates will change according to the work they plan

title: Radar Trends to Watch: November 2026
abstract: Coauthored with Claude Security looms large as we enter November. There’s been a lot of bad news: a certificate authority with woefully inadequate private keys, vulnerabilities have been discovered (and exploited) in PHP and other widely used programs, and several organizations have detected Chinese open weight models misbehaving in several different ways. New models are arriving faster and faster, and the best open-weight models are catching up to frontier model performance. But organizations that would like to achieve AI sovereignty will have to ask some difficult questions about the models they adopt. Is this an inflection point? Whether or not it is, AI has changed security permanently, and things are bound to get worse before they improve. AI models We are starting to see models developed with recursive self-improvement; we continue to see clones of Jev; and we’ve seen text watermarks added to output generated by Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s models. (Google has been using text watermarks for some time.) But tools for detecting the watermark are hard to find. Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s are in a very limited beta, and Google’s is only available in their enterprise package. What does a watermark mean if you can’t detect it? And, as we get more accustomed to AI-generated output, will anyone care? Kimi 3.1 Pro is a new open weight model with 3T tokens. On benchmarks, it is now the leading open weight model, only slightly behind the latest frontier models. Moonshot AI also released Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed, which is two to three times faster. Recursive has announced Flint , a 40B parameter mixture-of-experts model that activates 2.5B parameters per token. It was designed for coding, and sized to run on laptops. Flint is open weight; weights are available on Hugging Face , and it works with model runners like Ollama . Meta has shipped Muse Spark Open , an open weight model that they claim competes with the best Chinese open weight models. It’s a mixture-of-experts model with 816B parameters and 42B active parameters. Meta’s latest models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full , claim parity with frontier-class models. Specifically, they claim parity with Claude and ChatGPT for financial and legal work. The announcement hints that Meta will be using Muse to develop specialized models. OpenAI’s Decisions API is yet another Jev-like model. Like Jev, its input is a data structure that constrains the model’s output to be an answer to specific questions. The output is a data structure that includes a probability for each answer. Claude has launched Haiku 5.5, a new version of its least expensive model. It’s faster, less expensive, and has better benchmark scores than its predecessors. Haiku 5.5 is a very capable model, particularly for users who are sensitive to cost. Mistral has launched Mistral Large 4, a.k.a Le Chonk . It’s an open weight mixture-of-experts model with 1T parameters. It’s claimed to be the best open model from Europe and was designed with AI sovereignty in mind. Aleph Alpha has released an open weight LLM for English and German that was trained entirely under European rules. It is a mixture-of-experts model with 78B parameters. It uses a different tokenizing algorithm to handle long German words without breaking them into fragments. Reasoning takes place mostly in German. Crowdflare has released Clef and Clef Flash, new decision models that, like Jev, take typed queries and return typed answers about those queries. It’s also offering a new reinforcement learning service to help customers train Clef for their applications. After a long wait, Google has released two new frontier models, Gemini 4 Argon and Carbon . Argon is available to paying customers . Argon’s successor, Carbon, is being released slowly, and is currently only available via the Fairwind program.
